name: Exfoliating before tanning

lead: Exfoliating before self-tanner is a routine people use to get a smooth, even tan without patches or streaks. The aim is colour that looks natural rather than blotchy on elbows, knees and ankles.

Sunless tanners based on DHA react with amino acids in the dead outer layer of skin. The idea is that a smoother surface takes colour more uniformly. Tanning guides recommend it widely, though no study has compared prepared and unprepared skin.

paras: People scrub or otherwise exfoliate the body in a shower the day before, or shortly before, applying self-tanner, then apply the tan to clean, dry skin. It is a standard first step in most home self-tan routines.
Over-scrubbing can irritate skin, which is a general point about exfoliation rather than something specific to this routine. People with sensitive or broken skin tend to go gentler.

angle.text: Scrubbing off dead surface skin before self-tanner helps colour go on smoothly and avoid patches and streaks. DHA reacts in the dead outer layer, so a smoother surface is expected to take colour more evenly; the routine is common in tanning guides and has not been trialled.

lead: Exfoliating before tanning is the practice of removing dead surface skin, by scrubbing, using a mitt or applying acid exfoliants, before applying self-tanner. The aim is an even, natural-looking colour without streaks or patches, which is the main look-improvement people seek from the step.[1][2]

Sunless tanners based on dihydroxyacetone (DHA) are described as not being a dye: DHA reacts with amino acids in the dead outer layer of skin through browning reactions similar to those in food, and it does not need UV light.[1] The colour fades over about 3 to 10 days as that outer layer sheds.[1] Because the colour forms in the surface layer, practitioners reason that flaking or rough patches will hold more colour and show streaks, and that smoother skin takes colour more evenly.

Exfoliation itself is described as removing dead skin cells from the surface, either mechanically with scrubs, brushes or sponges or chemically with alpha- or beta-hydroxy acids or enzymes.[2] Dermatologists quoted in a general reference say exfoliation is not medically necessary because dead skin sheds naturally, and that over-exfoliating can weaken the skin barrier and cause redness and sensitivity.[2] No published trial has compared exfoliated and unexfoliated skin for self-tan evenness.

paras: Because DHA colour forms in the outer layer of dead skin and fades as that layer sheds over days,[1] practitioners describe removing flaking or rough patches first so colour is not patchy. This is a community and cosmetic-industry practice rather than a studied intervention.

DHA's tanning effect was noticed in the 1950s by Eva Wittgenstein at Cincinnati Children's Hospital after an oral treatment stained skin; the first commercial DHA self-tanner, Man-Tan, appeared in 1959, and Coppertone's QT followed in 1960, both giving orange tones that hurt the category's reputation.[1] Reformulations and, from the late 1990s, automated spray booths broadened the market.[1] Erythrulose, a common co-ingredient, works similarly but develops more slowly.[1]

Mechanical exfoliation uses abrasives such as scrubs, sugar or salt, loofahs, sponges and brushes; chemical exfoliation uses hydroxy acids or enzymes that loosen bonds between skin cells so they shed.[2] Removing dead cells can smooth skin texture and help products absorb better.[2]
Risks described include a weakened skin barrier, tightness, sensitivity and redness from excessive exfoliation, and environmental harm from plastic microbeads, which several places have banned.[2]

The FDA approves DHA for external use only, not around the eyes or lips or by inhalation.[1] A 2007 study found DHA-treated skin formed about 180 percent more free radicals during sun exposure than untreated skin, and sun protection is advised for at least a day after application.[1] DHA and erythrulose can cause contact dermatitis.[1]

No studies found comparing exfoliated and unexfoliated skin for self-tan evenness. Studies of DHA itself, including a 2007 study of free-radical formation and a 2004 cell study of DNA effects, are described in encyclopedic summaries.[1]

lore.intro: Preparing skin before self-tanner is commonly described in beauty and appearance discussions.

claims.claim: Exfoliating first gives a more even self-tan.
More scrubbing means a better base.

timeline.event: Man-Tan, the first commercial DHA self-tanner, is released.[1]
Automated spray booths broaden sunless tanning.[1]
